Course Overview
PVsyst is the reference simulation tool for bankable photovoltaic energy yield assessment. Lenders,
EPCs and independent engineers expect PVsyst outputs — P50/P90 yield, the loss diagram, and the
near-shading scene — as the technical backbone of a project's financial model. This curriculum
takes a practising engineer from a first grid-connected project through to defensible, audit-ready
energy assessments for utility-scale plants, with explicit attention to the assumptions reviewers
challenge most often.

Who This Is For
Solar design engineers, EPC technical staff, independent engineers, developers and asset
managers who must produce or interrogate PVsyst reports. Assumes working familiarity with PV
fundamentals; no prior PVsyst experience required.
Prerequisites
– Basic PV system concepts: modules, strings, inverters, DC/AC ratio
– Comfort with spreadsheets and basic statistics (mean, standard deviation, percentiles)
– Recommended: complete the Solar Design track first if you are new to PV
Learning Outcomes
On completion you will be able to:
1. Build a complete grid-connected PVsyst project from meteo import through to a signed simulation
report
2. Select, import and validate meteorological data, and defend the choice of data source in a
technical review
3. Construct 3D near-shading scenes for rooftop, fixed-tilt ground mount and single-axis tracker
plants
4. Configure detailed loss models — IAM, soiling, mismatch, thermal, ohmic, LID, degradation — with
justified values
5. Interpret the loss diagram line by line and diagnose a system that underperforms expectation
6. Run P50/P90/P99 uncertainty analysis and explain the variance components to a lender
7. Model bifacial gain, tracker backtracking and DC-coupled storage
8. Produce documentation that survives independent engineer review and cross-check it against
measured data

How to Use These Notes
PVsyst occupies an unusual position in the solar industry. It is not the most sophisticated modelling
tool available, nor the fastest, nor the most modern. It is simply the tool that lenders, independent
engineers and offtakers have agreed to accept, and that consensus makes fluency in it a
commercial requirement rather than a preference.
These notes are written accordingly. They assume you will produce reports that other people will
attack. Every section therefore does three things: it explains what PVsyst is calculating, it tells you
which inputs a reviewer will challenge, and it gives you the evidence you need to defend them.
A recurring theme: PVsyst will produce a beautifully formatted answer to a badly specified
question, and it will not warn you. The software validates syntax, not judgement. A project
created from a template with unpopulated loss parameters will simulate happily and produce a
performance ratio of 0.91, which is physically impossible, and nothing on screen will say so.
Learning where those traps sit is most of what separates a competent PVsyst user from a
dangerous one.
Prerequisites
These notes assume the content of the Solar Design track: solar geometry, module IV behaviour,
temperature coefficients, string sizing and the basic loss chain. Where a concept from that track is
needed it is recalled briefly, not re-derived.
Version Note
The content here reflects PVsyst 7.x. Menu paths and some default values changed between
versions 6 and 7, most notably in the bifacial model, the tracker backtracking implementation and
the handling of unavailability. When reading an older report, check the version stamp on the front
page before assuming any default.

Part I — Foundations and the PVsyst Data
Model
What PVsyst Actually Does
At its core PVsyst runs an hourly (or sub-hourly) energy balance over 8,760 time steps. For each
step it:
1. Reads meteorological data: GHI, DHI (or computes it), ambient temperature, wind speed.
2. Transposes horizontal irradiance to the plane of array using the Perez model.
3. Applies far (horizon) shading, then near shading from the 3D scene.
4. Applies the incidence angle modifier and soiling.
5. Computes cell temperature from the thermal model.
6. Solves the one-diode model for the array at that irradiance and temperature.
7. Applies module quality, LID and mismatch factors.
8. Applies electrical shading effects based on string layout.
9. Applies DC ohmic losses.
10. Applies the inverter model, including MPPT limits, efficiency curve and clipping.
11. Applies AC losses, transformer losses and auxiliary consumption.
12. Applies unavailability and any grid limitation.
The output is the loss diagram — a waterfall from incident global irradiation to energy injected into
the grid. Everything else in the report is a summary of that calculation.
KEY POINT
The loss diagram is the report. If you can read it line by line and justify every step, you understand
the model. If you cannot, you are transcribing software output rather than performing engineering.

Project Structure and File Hygiene
A PVsyst project contains:
· Site — geographic coordinates, altitude, time zone, albedo
· Meteo file — the hourly data, linked to a site
· Variants — individual simulation configurations within the project
· Components — modules, inverters, from the shared database
· 3D scene — shading geometry, stored per variant
Variant Discipline
Variants are the version control mechanism, and undisciplined variant naming is the most common
cause of confusion in a project handover. Adopt a convention and enforce it:
`` VC0 — Base case, all defaults, for reference VC1 — Meteo: Meteonorm 8.1 VC2 — VC1 + 3D
shading scene VC3 — VC2 + electrical shading with string assignment VC4 — VC3 + site-specific
soiling profile VC5 — Final for issue, rev A ``
Each variant should change one thing. When a reviewer asks "what did the shading scene cost
you?", the answer should be a subtraction between two adjacent variants, not a re-run.
COMMON ERROR
PVsyst does not lock variants. Anyone with the file can modify the variant that produced the issued
report. Export the report to PDF, archive the project file with a checksum, and record the variant
name and date in the report itself. Disputes about which configuration produced which number are
common and unpleasant.

The Time Zone Trap
If the meteo file's timestamps are offset from the site's solar time, PVsyst will compute solar
positions that do not match the irradiance data. The symptom is subtle: annual energy may be only
1–3% wrong, but the daily profile is skewed and, critically, the shading calculation is applied at the
wrong times of day.
Diagnostics:

· Plot the average daily irradiance profile from the meteo file. Its peak should sit at solar noon,
adjusted for the longitude offset from the standard meridian.
· Check whether the source data is in UTC, local standard time or local time with daylight saving.
Meteonorm, PVGIS and custom CSVs all differ.
· PVsyst offers a "check" on import that compares the measured profile against a clear-sky model.
Run it. It exists precisely for this.
WORKED EXAMPLE
Detecting a one-hour offset.
A site at longitude 12° E uses the CET standard meridian of 15° E. Solar noon therefore occurs at
12:00 CET + 4 min/° × (15 − 12) = 12:12 CET.
If the imported meteo file peaks at 13:12 in PVsyst's display, the data is in CEST (summer time) and
has not been converted. The consequence: morning shading is applied to afternoon hours and vice
versa. On a symmetric site the annual energy error may be under 1%, but on a site with an
obstruction to the east it can exceed 3%, and it will be in the wrong direction.
Albedo
PVsyst's default albedo is 0.20, applied as a constant across all months unless you specify monthly
values.
For a monofacial array, albedo affects only the ground-reflected term of the transposition and
typically influences annual GTI by well under 1%. For a bifacial array it is a first-order input — the
rear-side gain is close to proportional to it.

Structure of a standard PVsyst report.
The first three checks on any report you receive:
1. Performance ratio. Above 0.86 for a fixed-tilt plant is implausible. Above 0.88 is almost
certainly an unpopulated loss model.
2. Does a 3D scene exist? If the near-shading page says "no shadings" on a site with any
obstruction or any row spacing, the model is incomplete.
3. Is electrical shading enabled with string assignment? The report distinguishes "according
to strings" from "linear". Linear on a row-spaced ground mount understates shading loss
substantially.
SELF-TEST
1. A colleague sends a report with PR = 0.892 for a fixed-tilt plant in Spain. List, in order, the four
things you would check.
2. Explain why a one-hour time zone offset can produce a larger error on a site with an eastern
obstruction than on an unobstructed site.
3. What evidence would you require before accepting an albedo of 0.35 in a bifacial simulation?

Part II — Meteorological Data
The resource is the largest single source of uncertainty in a yield assessment and the first thing a
technical adviser examines. This part covers sourcing, importing, validating and defending
meteorological data.
What PVsyst Needs
Minimum required hourly (or monthly, which PVsyst will synthesise to hourly):
· GHI — global horizontal irradiance
· Ambient temperature
Strongly recommended:
· DHI — diffuse horizontal irradiance. If absent, PVsyst estimates it using the Erbs correlation from
the clearness index, which introduces additional uncertainty of roughly 1–2% on POA.
· Wind speed — required if you use a wind-dependent thermal model.
Optional: relative humidity, linke turbidity, albedo, rainfall.
KEY POINT
Supplying measured DHI rather than letting PVsyst derive it removes a meaningful uncertainty term.
If your data source offers DHI, use it, and say so in the report — reviewers notice.

The Site Adaptation Workflow
For a bankable project the accepted best practice combines a long-term satellite series with a short
ground measurement campaign.
1. Install a ground station: Class A pyranometer for GHI, ideally a second on the array plane, plus
ambient temperature and wind. Add a shaded pyranometer or RSI for DHI if budget allows.
2. Operate for a minimum of 12 months, with a documented cleaning and calibration regime.
3. Validate and clean the ground data: flag soiling periods, sensor faults, snow cover, levelling
errors.
4. Compare the concurrent period against the satellite series and derive a bias correction, typically a
simple multiplicative factor or a regression by clearness index.
5. Apply the correction to the full long-term satellite record.
6. Recompute the long-term mean and the interannual standard deviation from the corrected series.
The result reduces the resource uncertainty term from roughly 4–6% to 2.5–3.5%, which flows
directly into a higher P90.
WORKED EXAMPLE
Value of a site adaptation.
A 50 MWac project with P50 = 105,000 MWh/yr. Uncertainty components other than resource bias
combine to 4.4%.
Without adaptation: σbias = 5.0%, σtotal = √(25 + 19.36) = 6.66%
P90 = 105,000 × (1 − 1.282 × 0.0666) = 96,036 MWh
With adaptation: σbias = 3.0%, σtotal = √(9 + 19.36) = 5.33%
P90 = 105,000 × (1 − 1.282 × 0.0533) = 97,824 MWh
Gain: 1,788 MWh/yr of bankable energy. At $45/MWh and a 20-year debt tenor this is worth
several hundred thousand dollars in additional debt capacity, against a campaign cost of perhaps
$60,000–100,000. The business case is not close.

DC/AC Ratio Optimisation in PVsyst
PVsyst reports clipping as "Inverter loss over nominal inv. power" in the loss diagram.
The optimisation procedure:
1. Build variants at DC/AC ratios spanning 1.10 to 1.50 in steps of 0.05.
2. Record annual energy and clipping loss for each.
3. Compute the marginal energy gain per marginal MWdc added.
4. Compare against the marginal cost of that DC capacity.
5. Select the ratio where marginal value equals marginal cost, subject to any export limit.

COMMON ERROR

String Orientation Matters
For a shed-type ground mount, whether strings run along a row or across rows changes the shading
loss materially.
· Strings along the row (horizontal): a bottom-edge shadow affects the lowest module row
across many strings simultaneously — but only the modules in that row. If modules are in
landscape with the lower row on separate strings, loss is contained.
· Strings across rows (vertical): every string contains a module at the bottom edge, so every
string is affected by a bottom-edge shadow. This is markedly worse.
The design implication: on a row-spaced array where inter-row shading is expected, wire strings
horizontally along the row where the racking permits, so that shading is concentrated in a few
strings rather than spread across all of them.

Backtracking Mechanics
Without backtracking, at low sun elevations a tracker rotates to face the sun and shades the row
behind. PVsyst's backtracking algorithm limits rotation so that rows just avoid shading:
For ideal rotation angle Rideal:
if cos(Rideal) < GCR, backtrack to R such that cos(R) = GCR·cos(Rideal − ...)
The practical consequences:
· Backtracking eliminates near-shading loss between rows in the model — the near-shading line
goes to near zero.
· It reduces beam capture in the morning and evening, which appears as lower POA irradiation
rather than as a shading loss.
· Tighter GCR means more backtracking and less energy. The tracker gain is not a fixed
percentage; it depends on row spacing.

Bifacial gain sanity check.

East–West and Vertical Configurations
PVsyst handles east–west sheds through two subarrays with opposing azimuths. Points to note:
· Model them as separate subarrays on separate MPPTs. Combining them is both physically wrong
and electrically wrong.
· Mutual shading between the back-to-back rows must be in the 3D scene.
· The generation profile has two shoulders rather than one peak, which changes clipping behaviour
markedly — clipping is much lower for the same DC/AC ratio.
Vertical bifacial (modules mounted vertically, facing east and west) is increasingly used in
agrivoltaics and in snowy climates. PVsyst can model it as a 90° tilt with a bifacial rear, but the
unlimited-sheds assumption is stretched and results should be treated as approximate.

Economic Evaluation
Project > Economic evaluation
PVsyst includes a simple financial module: CAPEX by category, OPEX, tariff, discount rate, and a
resulting LCOE and payback.
It is adequate for a first pass and inadequate for a decision. It does not handle:
· Debt structuring, sculpted repayment, or DSCR
· Tax, depreciation or investment credits
· Time-varying tariffs beyond simple structures
· Inflation applied differently to CAPEX, OPEX and revenue
· Residual value
· Curtailment compensation
Use it to sanity-check a spreadsheet model, not to replace one. That said, its value is that the
energy series feeding it is the actual simulated hourly series, so if you export the hourly output to
your own model you get both rigour and flexibility.

Battery Sizing Discipline
The most common error is sizing the battery on average daily surplus. Daily surplus varies
enormously, and a battery sized on the mean is full on the days when it matters most.
Correct procedure:
1. Run the PV simulation without storage and export the hourly surplus series.
2. Build a duration curve of daily surplus energy.
3. Size the battery at a percentile appropriate to the objective — commonly P70–P80 of daily surplus
for self-consumption, or at the actual peak-shaving requirement for demand management.
4. Re-run with storage and verify the utilisation.
5. Check the cycle count against the warranty — a battery cycling twice daily reaches its cycle
warranty far sooner than one cycling once.

Once a plant operates, the model can be validated. The workflow:
1. Obtain measured data: AC energy at the meter, POA irradiance, module temperature, ambient

accepts a custom meteo file covering any period.
3. Apply actual availability and curtailment as recorded.
4. Compare measured against re-simulated energy.
5. Attribute the gap systematically.

WORKED EXAMPLE
Diagnosing a 7% shortfall.
A 20 MWp plant produces 7% less than the re-simulated model in its first year.
Step 1 — check the metering. Compare inverter-reported AC energy against the revenue meter. A CT
ratio error is rare but catastrophic and takes ten minutes to rule out. Result: agreement within
0.4%. Not metering.
Step 2 — check availability. Recorded downtime was 1.8% against 1.0% modelled. Accounts for
0.8%.
Step 3 — check PR by month. PR is close to model in winter and 9% below in summer. This seasonal
pattern points to a temperature or soiling issue, not a constant loss. Narrows the search.
Step 4 — check module temperature. Measured back-of-module temperature exceeds the model's
prediction by 6–8 °C at high irradiance. The array was installed with less rear clearance than
assumed, and the model used Uc = 29. Accounts for roughly 2.5%.
Step 5 — check string currents. 14 of 640 strings show currents below 90% of the array median.
Physical inspection finds connector faults on 11 and a damaged module on 3. Accounts for roughly
1.6%.
Step 6 — check soiling. Soiling station data shows 6.2% average against 3.5% modelled; the site is
downwind of a newly opened quarry. Accounts for roughly 2.2%.
Total attributed: 0.8 + 2.5 + 1.6 + 2.2 = 7.1%. The gap closes.
Actions. Revise the thermal model for future years, repair the string faults, renegotiate the cleaning
frequency, and update the long-term forecast. Note that only two of the four causes are recoverable
— the thermal issue is structural and permanent.
Performance Ratio Testing
Contractual PR tests follow IEC 61724 or ASTM E2848 methodology. Key points:
· Temperature correction is mandatory. An uncorrected PR test run in summer will fail and one
run in winter will pass, regardless of plant quality.
· Filtering criteria must be agreed in advance: minimum irradiance (commonly 400 or 600 W/m²),
stability criteria, exclusion of curtailed and unavailable periods.
· Measurement uncertainty must be stated; a PR test result of 0.802 ± 0.025 against a 0.80
guarantee is not a pass or a fail, it is a negotiation.

Appendix — Glossary and Quick Reference
Backtracking. Tracker control that rotates away from the ideal sun angle at low elevations to
prevent row-to-row shading.
Bifaciality factor. Ratio of rear to front efficiency of a bifacial module.
Clipping (overload loss). Energy lost when array output exceeds the inverter's AC rating.
Electrical shading. Additional loss beyond geometric shading, arising from bypass-diode and
series-string behaviour. Requires module layout to be defined.
Far shading. Shading from the distant horizon, entered as a height profile by azimuth.
GCR. Ground coverage ratio, collector width divided by row pitch.
IAM. Incidence angle modifier; reflection loss at oblique incidence.
LID. Light-induced degradation, a first-exposure power loss.
Loss diagram. PVsyst's waterfall from incident irradiation to grid energy. The core output of any
simulation.
Module layout. The assignment of physical modules in the 3D scene to electrical strings.
Prerequisite for electrical shading.
Near shading. Shading from objects in the 3D scene: rows, buildings, trees.
P50 / P90. Energy levels exceeded in 50% and 90% of years.
Perez model. The transposition model PVsyst uses by default to convert horizontal to
plane-of-array irradiance.
Preliminary Design. PVsyst's rapid monthly-resolution mode. Never for reports.
PR (performance ratio). Actual yield divided by the yield of a lossless STC-efficiency array under
the same POA irradiance.
Site adaptation. Correcting a long-term satellite series using a concurrent ground measurement
campaign.
TMY. Typical meteorological year.
Uc, Uv. Thermal model coefficients: constant and wind-dependent heat loss.
Unlimited sheds. The 2D assumption underlying PVsyst's bifacial model: infinitely long, infinitely
repeated rows over flat uniform ground.
Variant. A simulation configuration within a PVsyst project. The unit of version control.
